prompt: Some people argue that the primary role of education is to prepare students for employment, while others contend that schools should focus on personal development and critical thinking. Which view do you agree with more? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Schools are often judged by how quickly their graduates find work, so it is tempting to see education as job training. In my view, however, developing critical thinking and personal qualities should come first, because these abilities are what make a person employable over a whole career rather than for a single job.

Admittedly, the case for employment-focused schooling is strong. Families invest years and money in education, and they reasonably expect it to lead to a stable income. Practical subjects such as accounting, programming or technical drawing give young people skills that employers can use immediately, and a country with a well-trained workforce is more attractive to investors.

Nevertheless, specific job skills date quickly. A student trained only to operate today's software may find that the program has disappeared within a decade. By contrast, someone who has learnt to analyse evidence, solve unfamiliar problems and express ideas clearly can retrain when an industry changes. These are exactly the qualities that classes in literature, history and science develop when they ask pupils to question sources and defend their conclusions.

Furthermore, schools prepare citizens as well as workers. Young people need to manage money, judge the reliability of news and treat others with respect, and none of these abilities appears on a job description. A school that concentrates narrowly on employment risks producing capable technicians who are poorly equipped for adult life outside the office.

In conclusion, although preparing students for work is a legitimate aim, I believe the primary role of education is to build independent thinkers. Critical thinking and personal development are not alternatives to employability; in the long run, they are its foundation.
notes: Band 7: the introduction answers "which view do you agree with more" directly, the second paragraph concedes the other view fairly, and each later paragraph adds one new reason with a concrete example before the conclusion restates the same position.
band6: Nowadays education is very important for everyone. Some people think school is for getting a job and other people think it is for critical thinking. I agree with both because job is important and thinking is also important. For example, many students study IT because they want a good salary.

criteria.tr: Band 7 answers "which view do you agree with more" and keeps that answer to the end; the band-6 version sits on the fence ("I agree with both") and so never really answers the question.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each paragraph one job: concession, main reason, second reason, conclusion, linked by "Admittedly", "Nevertheless", "Furthermore". Band 6 runs both views into one paragraph with "and" and "also".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses precise collocations ("well-trained workforce", "date quickly", "independent thinkers"); band 6 repeats "important" and "job" and uses general nouns.
criteria.gra: Band 7 mixes relative clauses, conditionals and participle phrases accurately; band 6 has article slips ("because job is important") and mostly simple clauses.

prompt: Many believe that remote work has become the future of employment, while others maintain that physical offices remain essential. To what extent do you agree that remote work will replace traditional office environments? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
The rapid spread of remote work has led some commentators to predict the end of the traditional office. I agree only partly: remote work will become a permanent option for many employees, but I would argue that it will reshape offices rather than replace them.

There are clear reasons why working from home will last. Employees save the time and expense of commuting, and many find they can concentrate better without the interruptions of an open-plan floor. Employers, in turn, can recruit talent from a much wider area and reduce what they spend on rent. Once staff and managers have experienced these benefits, few organisations will return to a strict five-day office week.

However, offices perform functions that video calls cannot easily reproduce. New employees learn largely by watching experienced colleagues and asking quick questions, which is far harder through a screen. Creative work also depends on informal conversations that are rarely scheduled. In addition, some jobs, such as laboratory research or hospital administration, require shared equipment or a physical presence, and isolation at home can damage the wellbeing of people who live alone.

For these reasons, the most likely outcome is a hybrid model. Companies are already redesigning their premises as places for meetings, training and teamwork, while routine individual tasks are done at home. The office, in other words, is changing its purpose rather than disappearing.

In conclusion, remote work is here to stay, yet it will not fully replace the traditional workplace. On balance, I believe the future belongs to flexible arrangements in which employees divide their time between home and an office designed for collaboration.
notes: Band 7: answers "to what extent" with a qualified position (partly agree) stated in the introduction and repeated in the conclusion; one paragraph for each side, then a paragraph that resolves them into a hybrid model.
band6: In these days many companies let workers work from home. I think remote work is the future because it saves time and money. But some people like office because they can meet colleagues. In my opinion remote work will replace office soon because technology is very good now.

criteria.tr: Band 7 answers "to what extent" with a qualified position and explains why each side is partly right; band 6 gives an absolute claim ("will replace office soon") supported by one vague reason.
criteria.cc: Band 7 signals each step (There are clear reasons, However, For these reasons) and links back to the position; band 6 jumps between ideas without topic sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "hybrid model", "open-plan", "commuting", "physical presence"; band 6 repeats "office" and "remote work" without paraphrase.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses and concessive structures correctly; band 6 drops articles ("like office") and stays in the simple present.

prompt: Some people contend that governments should invest heavily in public transportation infrastructure, whereas others believe that improving road networks for private vehicles is more important. Do you agree or disagree with prioritising public transportation? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
As cities grow, governments must decide whether to spend transport budgets on public networks or on wider roads for private cars. I strongly agree that public transport should take priority, since it moves more people for less money and benefits a wider section of society.

The most convincing argument is efficiency. A single bus or train carriage carries as many passengers as dozens of cars, yet it occupies a fraction of the road space. Building more lanes, by contrast, tends to attract additional drivers, so congestion soon returns to its previous level. This effect, known as induced demand, explains why many cities that widened their motorways found traffic just as slow a few years later.

Public transport is also fairer. Elderly people, students and low-income workers often cannot afford a car or are unable to drive, and they depend on buses and trains to reach jobs, schools and hospitals. Investment in road networks mainly helps those who already own vehicles, whereas a good metro or bus system expands opportunities for everyone. Cleaner air and lower carbon emissions are further benefits shared by the whole population.

Admittedly, roads cannot be neglected. Goods are still delivered by lorry, and rural areas with scattered populations may never be served efficiently by trains. Governments should therefore maintain existing roads and fix dangerous junctions, but the bulk of new spending should go to public systems.

In conclusion, while some road investment remains necessary, I believe governments should prioritise public transportation. It reduces congestion more effectively than new roads, serves those who cannot drive, and delivers environmental benefits that private vehicles cannot match.
notes: Band 7: a strong, clear position in both the introduction and the conclusion, two developed reasons (efficiency, fairness) each with an explanation, and a concession paragraph that limits the claim without abandoning it.
band6: Transport is a big problem in many cities. I agree that government should spend money on public transport like buses and trains. Because more roads make more cars and traffic jam. Public transport is also cheaper for people and it is good for the environment too.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains why new roads fail ("induced demand") and supports the position with a developed example; band 6 states reasons as a list with no development.
criteria.cc: Band 7 builds one argument per paragraph with clear referencing ("This effect"); band 6 joins ideas with "also" and "too" in a single block.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "induced demand", "congestion", "carbon emissions", "scattered populations"; band 6 relies on "big problem" and "traffic jam".
criteria.gra: Band 7 has accurate complex sentences with relative and concessive clauses; band 6 has a sentence fragment ("Because more roads make more cars and traffic jam").

prompt: It is often argued that standardised testing is essential for evaluating student progress, while critics claim it narrows curricula and damages learning. Do you believe standardised testing is beneficial? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Standardised tests are used in many countries to measure what pupils have learnt and how well schools are performing. In my opinion, they are useful in moderation, but when they become the main goal of schooling they do more harm than good.

The benefits of standardised testing are real. Because every pupil answers the same questions under the same conditions, results can be compared fairly across schools and regions. This allows governments to identify schools that are struggling and direct extra resources to them. Moreover, tests can reveal gaps in basic skills, for example in reading or arithmetic, early enough for teachers to intervene.

However, problems arise when test scores are used to rank schools or to decide teachers' pay. Under this pressure, teachers naturally focus on what will be examined, a practice known as teaching to the test. Subjects that are not tested, such as art, music or practical science, receive less time, and lessons turn into rehearsals of past papers. Pupils may learn to recognise question types without understanding the ideas behind them, and anxious students can perform below their real ability.

The solution is not to abolish tests but to reduce their weight. Occasional national assessments based on samples of pupils would still give governments the information they need, while teachers' own assessment of projects and coursework would reward deeper learning.

In conclusion, I believe standardised testing is beneficial as one source of information about pupils' progress. It should not, however, dominate the curriculum, because a high-stakes testing system narrows what children learn and undermines the very achievement it is meant to measure.
notes: Band 7: the position (useful in moderation) is precise and consistent; one paragraph gives the benefits fairly, the next explains the mechanism of harm, and a short paragraph offers a practical middle way before the conclusion.
band6: Standardised tests are used in many schools around the world. They have advantages and disadvantages. The advantage is that teachers can compare students easily. The disadvantage is that students only study for the test and they feel stress. In my opinion tests are good but not too much.

criteria.tr: Band 7 takes a clear, qualified position on whether testing is beneficial and explains how high stakes narrow the curriculum; band 6 lists one pro and one con and gives a vague position ("not too much").
criteria.cc: Band 7 moves from benefits to problems to solution with purposeful linking; band 6 uses the formula "The advantage is... The disadvantage is...".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "teaching to the test", "high-stakes", "intervene", "coursework"; band 6 repeats "test" and "students".
criteria.gra: Band 7 controls complex noun phrases and passive forms; band 6 is mostly simple sentences.

prompt: Some argue that cultural heritage sites should prioritise preservation over public access, while others believe they should remain open to tourists regardless of conservation costs. Which position do you support? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Historic sites such as ancient temples and medieval castles attract millions of visitors, but heavy footfall can damage the very features people come to see. In my view, preservation must come first, although this does not mean closing sites; it means managing access so that they survive for future generations.

Those who favour open access make valid points. Ticket sales and tourist spending fund restoration work that might otherwise be unaffordable, and local communities that earn a living from visitors have a strong incentive to protect their heritage. Moreover, these places belong to humanity as a whole, and allowing people to experience them directly encourages public support for conservation.

Nevertheless, unlimited access is self-defeating. Stone steps are worn away by constant walking, the breath and body heat of crowds alter the humidity inside painted caves and tombs, and litter and graffiti accumulate. Once original material is lost, no amount of money can bring it back. If sites remain open regardless of conservation costs, today's visitors are effectively consuming what should be passed on.

A sensible compromise is controlled access. Daily visitor caps, timed tickets and raised walkways allow people to enjoy a site while limiting erosion. The most fragile areas can be closed and replaced with accurate replicas or virtual tours, an approach that has allowed the public to see copies of famous prehistoric cave paintings without endangering the originals.

In conclusion, I support the view that preservation should take priority. Tourism and conservation can coexist, but only when access is carefully limited, because a damaged monument benefits neither visitors nor future generations.
notes: Band 7: the introduction chooses a side and immediately refines it (preservation first, but managed access rather than closure); the opposing view is treated fairly before being answered, and the compromise paragraph shows how the position works in practice.
band6: Heritage sites are very old and famous places like temples and castles. Some people say we should close them to protect them. Other people say tourists should visit them. I think tourists should visit because they bring money. But too many tourists can damage the sites, so it is a problem.

criteria.tr: Band 7 chooses a side and shows how managed access protects sites; band 6 picks a side and then undercuts it ("so it is a problem") without resolving the conflict.
criteria.cc: Band 7 structures a fair counter-argument followed by a rebuttal and a compromise; band 6 ends on a new problem instead of a conclusion.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "visitor caps", "erosion", "timed tickets", "replicas"; band 6 uses "very old", "famous places", "problem".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses conditionals and passives accurately ("Once original material is lost"); band 6 relies on simple sentences joined by "so".

prompt: Some people believe that prison should primarily focus on rehabilitation and reintegration of offenders, whereas others argue that punishment and deterrence are more important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Societies disagree about what prisons are for. Some people believe their main purpose is to reform offenders, while others argue that punishment and deterrence matter more. This essay discusses both positions, but I would argue that rehabilitation should be the priority because it protects the public more effectively in the long term.

Supporters of punishment make an understandable case. Victims and their families want to see justice done, and a prison sentence expresses society's condemnation of serious crime. Advocates also believe that the threat of harsh sentences discourages potential offenders, and that locking up dangerous individuals keeps communities safe, at least for as long as they remain inside.

On the other hand, almost every prisoner is eventually released, so the crucial question is what kind of person leaves the prison gate. Many offenders lack education, have no work history or struggle with addiction or mental illness. If a sentence does nothing to address these problems, they are likely to return to crime, and the cycle of arrest and imprisonment continues at great public expense. Prisons that offer schooling, vocational training and treatment, by contrast, give inmates a realistic chance of finding a job and a home after release.

In my view, rehabilitation does not mean ignoring punishment. Losing one's freedom is itself a serious penalty, and violent offenders must be held securely. However, the time spent in custody should be used to reduce the risk of reoffending, since that is what ultimately prevents future victims.

In conclusion, both deterrence and reform have a place in the justice system. On balance, however, I believe prisons should focus primarily on rehabilitation, because reducing reoffending serves both public safety and the interests of justice better than punishment alone.
notes: Band 7: both views get a developed paragraph before the opinion is defended; the key move is the reframing that most prisoners are released, which turns the debate into a question of public safety.
band6: Prison is a place for criminals. Some people think prison should help criminals to change their life. Other people think prison should punish them so they do not do crime again. Both ideas have good points. I think rehabilitation is better because criminals can get a job after prison.

criteria.tr: Band 7 discusses both views fully and gives a reasoned opinion in the introduction and conclusion; band 6 summarises each view in one sentence and supports its opinion with a single undeveloped reason.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each view its own paragraph and links the opinion back to both; band 6 compresses all views into one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "reoffending", "deterrence", "vocational training", "in custody"; band 6 uses "criminals", "do crime", "change their life".
criteria.gra: Band 7 varies structures (conditionals, relative clauses, passive); band 6 uses short repetitive patterns ("Some people think... Other people think").

prompt: Some argue that technology is rapidly eliminating the need for traditional crafts and manual skills, while others believe these skills remain valuable and should be preserved. Discuss both sides and state your opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Machines now produce furniture, clothing and pottery faster and more cheaply than any craftsperson. Some people therefore argue that traditional crafts and manual skills are becoming obsolete, whereas others believe these skills are still valuable. I believe they should be preserved, although their role has changed from meeting everyday needs to sustaining culture and quality.

It is true that technology has removed the economic necessity of many crafts. A factory can make thousands of identical chairs in the time a carpenter makes one, and consumers understandably choose the cheaper product. Similarly, computer-aided design and automated tools have replaced many skilled tasks in manufacturing. From a purely economic standpoint, it is difficult to justify training large numbers of young people in hand weaving or blacksmithing.

Nevertheless, crafts carry value that price alone does not capture. They are part of a community's identity: traditional textiles, carving and metalwork express local history in a way mass-produced goods cannot. Hand skills also support a growing market for artisanal products, as many buyers are willing to pay more for items that are unique and durable. In addition, manual work develops patience, precision and problem-solving, and practical abilities such as plumbing or electrical repair remain essential precisely because machines cannot do them in people's homes.

Preservation does not have to be expensive. Museums and schools can run workshops, governments can recognise master craftspeople, and online platforms allow small makers to reach customers worldwide.

In conclusion, although technology has reduced the economic need for many traditional skills, I am convinced they should be protected. They preserve cultural heritage, meet a genuine demand for quality and keep practical competence alive in an increasingly automated world.
notes: Band 7: the opposing view is accepted on its own terms (economics) before the essay shifts to values that economics misses; the position is stated in the introduction with a clear qualification and repeated in the conclusion.
band6: Technology is growing very fast and machines can do many jobs now. So some people think crafts like weaving are not needed. But I think crafts are still important because they are part of culture and tourists like to buy them. Also people enjoy making things by hand in their free time.

criteria.tr: Band 7 separates economic need from cultural value and evaluates both views; band 6 dismisses one view in a sentence and lists reasons for the other.
criteria.cc: Band 7 builds a clear progression from the first view to the second and then to practical steps; band 6 strings reasons together with "Also" and "But".
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "obsolete", "artisanal", "mass-produced", "master craftspeople"; band 6 uses "things", "important", "very fast".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses concession and relative clauses accurately; band 6 starts sentences with "So" and "But" and stays simple.

prompt: Some people believe that animal testing in medical research is necessary and justified, whereas others argue that alternative methods should replace it entirely. Discuss both perspectives and share your opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
The use of animals in medical research divides opinion sharply. Some people regard it as a necessary price for safe medicines, while others insist that it should be replaced completely by other techniques. In my opinion, animal testing should be reduced as quickly as science allows, but it cannot yet be abolished without putting patients at risk.

Those who defend animal research point to its record. For example, many vaccines, surgical techniques and treatments for serious diseases were developed with the help of animal studies. A living body is extremely complex: a drug may seem harmless to cells in a dish yet damage the liver or heart once it circulates through a whole organism. For this reason, most regulators still require animal data before a new medicine is tested on human volunteers.

Opponents, on the other hand, stress the suffering involved and question how reliable the results are. Animals are not small humans, and as a result some substances that were safe in mice have proved harmful to people. Meanwhile, alternatives are improving rapidly. Human tissue grown in the laboratory, "organ-on-a-chip" devices and computer modelling can already replace certain tests, and they may eventually predict human reactions more accurately than animals do.

Weighing these arguments, I believe the sensible path lies between the two extremes. Testing for cosmetics and other non-essential products should be banned, and every experiment should be justified as necessary. At the same time, governments should fund alternative methods so that animal use can be phased out as these technologies are proven.

In conclusion, animal testing remains necessary for some medical research today, but it should not be accepted as permanent. Investment in alternatives must continue until they can replace it altogether.
notes: Band 7: each perspective is explained with a mechanism (why whole organisms matter; why animal results can mislead), and the opinion is conditional but clear: reduce now, replace when alternatives are proven.
band6: Animal testing is a controversial topic. Some people think it is necessary for medicine because we need to know if new drugs are safe. Other people think it is cruel to animals and we can use computers instead. In my opinion animal testing is necessary but we should reduce it.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains why current alternatives cannot fully replace testing yet and gives a clear conditional position; band 6 has a position ("necessary but we should reduce it") but no explanation of why.
criteria.cc: Band 7 develops each perspective in its own paragraph before weighing them; band 6 condenses both into two sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "organ-on-a-chip", "computer modelling", "regulators", "phased out"; band 6 relies on "cruel" and "necessary".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses complex hedged statements and passives accurately; band 6 is accurate but almost entirely simple and compound sentences.

prompt: Some argue that children should learn predominantly through play and exploration, while others maintain that structured traditional teaching is essential for academic achievement. Discuss both views and give your opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Educators have long debated whether children learn best through free play and exploration or through structured lessons led by a teacher. Both approaches have merits, but I believe the balance should shift with age: play should dominate in the early years, while structured teaching should grow in importance as children get older.

Advocates of play-based learning argue that young children learn most naturally by doing. For instance, building with blocks teaches basic ideas about balance and number, and role-play develops vocabulary and social skills. Because children choose their own activities, they stay curious and motivated, and they learn to cooperate and solve problems without being told what to do. Pushing very young pupils into formal desk work, supporters say, can make them anxious and turn them against school.

Supporters of traditional teaching reply that some knowledge does not emerge from play. Reading, spelling and arithmetic depend on systematic practice, and a skilled teacher can explain in minutes a rule that a child might never discover alone. In addition, clear instruction helps pupils from homes with few books or educational toys, who may otherwise fall behind their classmates.

In my view, these positions are less opposed than they seem. In kindergarten, carefully planned play can introduce letters and numbers, and teachers can guide it with questions. As pupils move through primary school, more explicit instruction is needed to build literacy and numeracy, although practical projects should remain part of the timetable to keep learning engaging.

In conclusion, neither extreme serves children well. I would argue that education should begin with guided play and gradually introduce more structured teaching, so that children gain both curiosity and the solid academic foundations they need.
notes: Band 7: both views are developed with concrete classroom examples, and the opinion is not a vague "both are good" but a specific, staged answer (play first, more structure later) stated in the introduction and conclusion.
band6: Children learn in different ways. Some people think play is the best way to learn because children are happy. Others think teachers should teach in a traditional way so children get good marks. I think both are good. Young children should play and older children should study more.

criteria.tr: Band 7 develops a staged view with reasons for why play suits early years and instruction suits later ones; band 6 has the same idea but states it in one undeveloped sentence.
criteria.cc: Band 7 links each paragraph to the next stage of the argument ("Supporters of traditional teaching reply"); band 6 lists views without transitions.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "role-play", "systematic practice", "literacy and numeracy", "explicit instruction"; band 6 uses "good", "happy", "good marks".
criteria.gra: Band 7 varies sentence openings and uses comparatives accurately; band 6 repeats subject-verb-object patterns.

prompt: Urban migration—the movement of people from rural to urban areas—offers various advantages and disadvantages. Discuss both and determine whether the advantages outweigh the disadvantages. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Across the developing world, millions of people are leaving the countryside to live in towns and cities. This movement brings significant benefits for migrants and national economies, but it also creates serious problems in both urban and rural areas. On balance, I believe the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that governments plan for growth.

The main advantage is economic opportunity. Cities offer a far wider range of jobs than villages, and wages are generally higher, so migrants can escape poverty and send money home to relatives. Urban areas also provide better access to hospitals, universities and public services, which allows the children of migrants to receive an education their parents never had. For the country as a whole, concentrating workers in cities encourages new businesses and industries to develop.

However, rapid migration places heavy pressure on cities. Housing often fails to keep pace with demand, so many newcomers end up in crowded informal settlements without clean water or sanitation. Traffic, pollution and competition for jobs can worsen as populations grow. Meanwhile, rural areas lose many of their young people, leaving farms short of labour and villages populated mainly by the elderly.

These problems are serious, yet most of them can be managed. Investment in affordable housing and public transport can make urban growth more orderly, and improving roads, schools and internet access in the countryside can reduce the pressure to leave. By contrast, the opportunities that cities create for individuals are difficult to provide in any other way.

In conclusion, rural-to-urban migration has real costs, including overcrowded cities and declining villages. Nevertheless, I believe its advantages outweigh its disadvantages, because it offers people a route out of poverty that rural areas usually cannot.
notes: Band 7: the question "do the advantages outweigh" is answered in the introduction with a condition, both sides are developed with consequences, and the fourth paragraph explains why the disadvantages are more manageable, which is the actual weighing.
band6: Many people move from village to city to find work. The advantage is they can get more money and better hospitals. The disadvantage is cities become crowded and villages have only old people. I think advantages are more than disadvantages because people have better life in the city.

criteria.tr: Band 7 weighs the two sides and explains why the disadvantages are more manageable; band 6 states that advantages are "more than disadvantages" without weighing them.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each side a developed paragraph and then a weighing paragraph; band 6 uses one sentence per side.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "informal settlements", "sanitation", "short of labour", "orderly"; band 6 uses "village", "crowded", "better life".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses comparative structures and conditionals accurately; band 6 has article omissions ("from village to city").

prompt: Automation and artificial intelligence bring both benefits and challenges to modern workplaces. Analyse these advantages and disadvantages and determine whether they ultimately benefit society more than they harm it. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Automation and artificial intelligence are changing how work is done in factories, offices and hospitals. These technologies offer large gains in productivity and safety, yet they also threaten many jobs. I would argue that they will benefit society more than they harm it, but only if the gains are shared and displaced workers are supported.

The advantages are considerable. Machines can work continuously without fatigue, which lowers production costs and can make goods and services cheaper for consumers. Dangerous tasks, such as handling chemicals or inspecting mines, can be transferred to robots, reducing workplace injuries. Artificial intelligence can also process enormous quantities of information, helping doctors detect diseases earlier and engineers identify faults before they cause accidents.

On the other hand, the disadvantages fall heavily on particular groups. Workers in routine roles, from assembly lines to call centres and data entry, may find their skills no longer needed. Even if new jobs appear elsewhere, they often require different qualifications and may be located in other regions, so an older factory worker cannot simply move into software development. Furthermore, if the profits from automation go mainly to the owners of technology, inequality is likely to widen.

Whether the overall effect is positive therefore depends on policy rather than on the machines themselves. Governments and employers should invest in retraining programmes, adapt school curricula to the skills that machines cannot easily copy, such as creativity and care work, and ensure that tax systems capture part of the productivity gains for public services.

In conclusion, automation brings real dangers for workers whose jobs disappear. Nevertheless, I believe its benefits for society outweigh its harms, as long as the transition is managed so that the people who lose out are given a fair chance to adapt.
notes: Band 7: the answer to "more benefit or more harm" appears in the introduction and conclusion with a clear condition; the disadvantages paragraph explains why displaced workers cannot easily switch jobs, which gives the weighing real substance.
band6: AI and robots are used in many workplaces now. They make work faster and companies save money. But many workers lose their jobs and they are worried. In my opinion AI is more good than bad because new jobs will come, for example jobs in computer programming.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains who gains, who loses and what makes the overall effect positive; band 6 asserts that "new jobs will come" without support.
criteria.cc: Band 7 balances the two sides in separate paragraphs before a paragraph on what decides the outcome; band 6 moves straight to opinion after two sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "productivity", "displaced workers", "retraining programmes", "inequality"; band 6 has a word-form error ("more good than bad").
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses conditionals and passives naturally ("can be transferred", "if the profits... go"); band 6 is mostly simple present.

prompt: Working from home has become increasingly common in recent years, offering both benefits and drawbacks for employees and employers. Evaluate both advantages and disadvantages and decide whether the overall impact is positive or negative. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Working from home, once unusual, has become a normal arrangement for many office staff. It brings clear benefits to both employees and employers, but it also creates difficulties that are easy to underestimate. In my view, its overall impact is positive, provided that organisations combine it with regular time in the workplace.

For employees, the most obvious gain is the end of the daily commute. The time and money saved can be spent on family, exercise or rest, and parents and carers find it easier to combine work with their responsibilities. Many people also concentrate better at home than in a noisy open-plan office. Employers benefit too: they can reduce spending on office space and recruit staff who live far from the company's base.

However, there are significant drawbacks. Employees who work alone every day may feel isolated, and the boundary between work and private life can disappear when the laptop is always on the kitchen table. Junior staff often suffer most, as they lose the chance to learn by observing experienced colleagues. For employers, it is harder to build team spirit and to share ideas informally, and some managers struggle to supervise people they rarely see.

Most of these problems, however, arise from working at home all the time rather than some of the time. A hybrid pattern, in which staff spend part of the week together for meetings and training, keeps most of the flexibility while protecting collaboration and mentoring.

In conclusion, remote work has both strengths and weaknesses for staff and companies. On balance, I believe its impact is positive, as long as it is organised as a flexible mix of home and office working rather than complete separation.
notes: Band 7: advantages and disadvantages are both organised by stakeholder (employees, then employers), and the fourth paragraph explains why most drawbacks are manageable, which justifies the positive judgement given in the introduction and conclusion.
band6: Working from home is popular after the pandemic. For employees it is good because they do not need to travel and they have more time with family. For employers it is bad because they cannot check workers. I think it is positive for everyone because people are more happy.

criteria.tr: Band 7 evaluates both groups and reaches a qualified judgement; band 6 says "positive for everyone" despite listing an employer drawback.
criteria.cc: Band 7 groups ideas by stakeholder with clear topic sentences; band 6 mixes stakeholders in one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses "commute", "open-plan", "isolated", "mentoring", "supervise"; band 6 uses "good", "bad", "check workers".
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses complex comparison and relative clauses; band 6 has a comparative error ("more happy").

prompt: International tourism brings both positive and negative consequences to host countries. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages and determine whether tourism is ultimately more beneficial than harmful to local communities. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
International tourism is one of the largest industries in the world, and many countries actively compete for foreign visitors. Tourism brings income and employment, but it can also damage the environment and the daily lives of local residents. I believe it is more beneficial than harmful, but only where communities share the profits and visitor numbers are controlled.

The economic advantages are the most visible. Hotels, restaurants, guides and transport companies all create jobs, often in regions with few other industries. Visitors spend foreign currency, and governments can use the resulting tax revenue to improve roads, airports and public services that residents also use. Tourism can also encourage the preservation of traditional crafts, festivals and historic buildings, because these attract visitors.

However, the costs are frequently borne by the people who benefit least. Popular destinations can become so crowded that residents are priced out of their own neighbourhoods as homes are converted into holiday rentals. Beaches, coral reefs and mountain trails suffer from pollution and erosion, and scarce water supplies may be diverted to hotels and golf courses. Furthermore, when resorts are owned by international companies, much of the money spent by tourists leaves the country instead of supporting local businesses.

These harms are serious, but they are not inevitable. Local ownership of guesthouses and tour services keeps income within the community, and limits on cruise ships or holiday lets can prevent overtourism. Some islands, for instance, charge visitors an entry fee that funds conservation.

In conclusion, tourism can strain host communities when it is unmanaged. On balance, though, I believe its benefits outweigh its drawbacks, provided that governments regulate visitor numbers and ensure local people receive a fair share of the income.

prompt: Many cities face severe traffic congestion problems. What are the causes of this issue and what measures might reduce congestion effectively? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Traffic congestion wastes time, raises pollution levels and makes city life stressful. It has several connected causes, and in my view it can only be reduced by measures that make driving less attractive and the alternatives more attractive at the same time.

The first cause is the sheer growth in car ownership. As incomes rise, more households buy vehicles, and many treat the car as the default choice for every journey, even short ones. In addition, the way cities are planned plays a part. When homes are built in distant suburbs and jobs are concentrated in the centre, large numbers of people must travel in the same direction at the same time. Finally, where public transport is slow, unreliable or overcrowded, commuters have little reason to leave their cars at home.

Although building more roads might seem the obvious answer, extra lanes tend to attract more drivers and, as a result, soon fill up again. Therefore, a more effective approach has three parts. First, governments should invest in fast and frequent public transport, such as metro lines and dedicated bus lanes, so that it can compete with driving. Second, drivers should pay for the space they use, for example through congestion charges in city centres or higher parking fees. Cities that have introduced such charges have generally seen fewer cars entering the centre. Third, planners should place housing, shops and offices closer together so that more trips can be made on foot or by bicycle.

In conclusion, congestion results from rising car ownership, poor urban planning and weak public transport. I believe governments must tackle these causes together, combining better alternatives with charges on driving, rather than relying on new roads that only postpone the problem.
notes: Band 7: one paragraph explains three causes, the next matches a solution to each, and the essay explicitly rejects the obvious but ineffective solution (more roads), which shows evaluation rather than listing.

prompt: Social media addiction is becoming increasingly prevalent, particularly among young people. Identify the causes of this phenomenon and suggest practical solutions to address it. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Many young people now spend several hours a day scrolling through social media, often feeling unable to stop. This compulsive use has identifiable causes in the design of the apps and in the lives of teenagers, and I believe it should be tackled by technology companies, schools and families together.

The most important cause lies in how platforms are built. Their business model depends on advertising, so they earn more when users stay longer. Features such as infinite scrolling, autoplay videos and constant notifications are designed to remove natural stopping points, while likes and comments provide small, unpredictable rewards that keep people checking their phones. Young people are especially vulnerable, partly because self-control is still developing during adolescence and partly because approval from peers matters so much at that age. Fear of missing out on conversations and events makes it hard for a teenager to log off when everyone else is online.

Solutions must therefore address both design and habits, as well as the needs behind them. For example, governments could require platforms to switch off autoplay and night-time notifications by default for younger users and to show clear screen-time summaries. Schools should teach digital literacy, helping students understand how apps capture attention so that they can make more conscious choices. At home, parents can agree on simple rules, such as keeping phones out of bedrooms at night, and set an example by limiting their own use. Finally, young people need attractive offline alternatives, such as sports clubs and creative activities, that offer the social connection they seek online.

In conclusion, although individual willpower matters, social media overuse among the young is driven largely by deliberate design and by the strong need for peer approval in adolescence. To reduce it, regulation of platform features must be combined with education and practical changes in family routines.

prompt: Homelessness remains a persistent problem in many developed nations. What factors contribute to this issue and what practical measures could governments implement to address it effectively? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Even in wealthy countries, many people sleep on the streets or move between shelters and friends' sofas. Homelessness has both structural and personal causes, and I believe governments should respond with a combination of affordable housing and targeted support services.

The most fundamental cause is the cost of housing. In many cities, rents and property prices have risen much faster than wages, and as a result people on low incomes spend most of their earnings on accommodation. A sudden shock, such as losing a job, a relationship breakdown or an unexpected bill, can then lead to eviction. In addition, personal difficulties play a part. Mental illness, addiction and domestic violence can make it hard for people to keep a tenancy, and young people leaving care or prison often have no family to fall back on. Moreover, these factors usually reinforce each other: life on the street worsens health problems, which in turn makes it harder to find work and housing.

Governments can address these causes in several practical ways. First, they should increase the supply of affordable homes, either by building social housing directly or by requiring developers to include low-cost units in new projects. Second, a "housing first" approach, which gives homeless people a stable home before asking them to solve other problems, has proved more successful in several countries than making housing conditional on recovery. Third, support services such as mental health care, addiction treatment and job training should be linked to housing rather than offered separately. Finally, prevention is cheaper than cure; therefore, emergency grants and legal advice for tenants facing eviction can stop many people from becoming homeless in the first place.

In conclusion, homelessness results from expensive housing combined with personal vulnerabilities. To reduce it effectively, governments must provide affordable homes and integrated support, and intervene early before people lose their accommodation.

prompt: Food waste has become a significant environmental and social problem in many countries. What are the principal causes of food waste and what practical solutions would address this issue? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Large quantities of edible food are thrown away every day, while many people still cannot afford a healthy diet. This waste also squanders the water, land and energy used to produce it. In my view, the problem has causes at every stage of the food chain, so solutions must involve farmers, retailers and households alike.

On farms, waste often occurs before food even reaches a shop. Supermarkets tend to reject fruit and vegetables that are misshapen or the wrong size, so perfectly nutritious produce is left in the fields. In poorer regions, a lack of refrigerated storage and good roads means that harvested crops spoil before they reach markets. Further along the chain, shops overstock their shelves to look abundant and then discard items as they near their sell-by dates.

In wealthy countries, however, the largest share of waste comes from households. Large packs and multi-buy offers encourage people to purchase more than they need, and confusion between "best before" and "use by" labels leads many families to throw out food that is still safe to eat. In addition, busy lifestyles mean that meals are not planned, so ingredients are forgotten at the back of the fridge.

Each of these causes, therefore, suggests a practical remedy. Retailers should relax cosmetic standards and sell imperfect produce at lower prices, and governments can encourage supermarkets to donate unsold food to charities by protecting them from legal liability. Investment in cold storage would greatly reduce losses in developing countries. As for consumers, clearer date labels, smaller pack sizes and public campaigns on meal planning and using leftovers would make a significant difference.

In conclusion, food waste stems from strict retail standards, poor storage and household habits. I believe it should be tackled at every stage, through better infrastructure, changes in retail practice and clearer information for consumers.

prompt: Some believe that governments should prioritise spending on environmental protection even if it reduces other public expenditures, while others argue that economic development should come first. How important is environmental protection compared to economic growth? What specific steps should governments take to balance these priorities? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Governments face constant pressure to choose between protecting the environment and promoting economic growth. In my view, environmental protection is at least as important as growth, because a damaged environment eventually undermines the economy itself, and governments should pursue policies that serve both aims.

The importance of the environment becomes clear when its economic role is considered. Agriculture depends on fertile soil and stable rainfall, fisheries depend on healthy seas, and tourism depends on clean beaches and forests. Pollution also imposes direct costs, as illnesses caused by dirty air and water reduce productivity and raise healthcare spending. Moreover, climate change threatens to destroy infrastructure through floods and storms. Growth achieved by exhausting these resources is therefore short-lived. It is true that poorer countries need development urgently to reduce poverty, but this is an argument for cleaner growth, not for ignoring environmental damage.

To balance these priorities, governments can take several concrete steps. First, they should make polluters pay, for example through a carbon tax or charges on industrial waste, so that companies have a financial reason to adopt cleaner methods. The revenue can be used to reduce other taxes or to help low-income households with higher energy costs. Second, public investment should be directed towards renewable energy, efficient public transport and the insulation of buildings, all of which create jobs while cutting emissions. Third, environmental regulations should be predictable and phased in gradually, giving businesses time to adapt instead of facing sudden costs.

In conclusion, environmental protection should not be treated as a luxury that comes after growth. I believe governments must recognise that long-term prosperity depends on a healthy environment and use taxation, investment and clear regulation to achieve both goals together.

prompt: Many developed nations are experiencing ageing populations as birth rates decline. What are the consequences of population ageing for societies and economies? What measures should governments implement to address these challenges? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
In many developed countries, people are living longer while fewer children are being born, so the average age of the population is rising. This shift has serious economic and social consequences, and I believe governments must respond with a range of measures rather than a single policy.

The most significant economic consequence is the pressure on public finances. As the proportion of retired people grows, the cost of pensions and healthcare increases, while the number of working-age taxpayers who fund these services shrinks. Employers may also face labour shortages, particularly in sectors such as construction and nursing, which can slow economic growth. In addition, the demand for long-term care rises sharply. Because families are smaller and often live far apart, many older people cannot rely on relatives for support, and the burden shifts to the state or to private care homes that many cannot afford.

Governments can take several steps to address these challenges. First, the retirement age can be raised gradually in line with life expectancy, and flexible arrangements can encourage healthy older people to keep working part-time. Second, family-friendly policies, such as affordable childcare and paid parental leave, may help couples who want children to have them, although their effect on birth rates tends to be modest. Moreover, carefully managed immigration of working-age people can fill gaps in the labour market. Finally, investment in preventive healthcare would help people remain healthy and independent for longer, reducing the need for expensive treatment and residential care.

In conclusion, an ageing population strains public budgets, the labour market and care services. To meet these challenges, governments should combine later and more flexible retirement, support for families, managed immigration and preventive healthcare, since no single measure will be sufficient on its own.

criteria.gra: Band 7 is accurate across complex sentences; band 6 has countable-noun errors ("less babies", "less workers").

prompt: Linguistic diversity is declining as more people learn English as a global lingua franca. Is this language loss a problem for humanity? What steps could be taken to preserve endangered languages and cultural diversity? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
As English spreads as the shared language of business, science and the internet, many smaller languages are spoken by fewer people each generation. In my opinion, this loss is a genuine problem for humanity, and governments and communities should act to keep endangered languages alive.

A language is far more than a means of communication. It carries a community's stories, songs, humour and ways of understanding the world. Many indigenous languages, for example, contain detailed knowledge of local plants, animals and weather that has never been written down in any other form. When the last fluent speakers die, this knowledge usually disappears with them. In addition, language loss can damage the identity and confidence of a community, especially when people were once discouraged or even punished for speaking their mother tongue. Admittedly, a common language such as English brings real benefits, allowing people from different countries to trade, study and cooperate. However, these benefits do not require other languages to die, since people can be bilingual.

Therefore, several steps could help preserve linguistic diversity. First, schools in areas with minority languages should offer bilingual education, so that children learn their heritage language alongside the national language and English. Second, governments can give endangered languages official recognition and support media in them, such as radio stations, television programmes and online content, which make the language part of modern life rather than a relic. Third, linguists and community members should record elderly speakers and create dictionaries and digital archives. Finally, the most effective revitalisation projects are led by the communities themselves, so funding should support local initiatives rather than impose plans from outside.

In conclusion, the decline of linguistic diversity represents a loss of knowledge and identity that cannot easily be recovered. I believe it should be countered through bilingual education, official support and community-led documentation.
notes: Band 7: the first question is answered with a clear position and specific reasons (knowledge, identity), the opposing benefit of English is acknowledged and answered, and the steps paragraph moves from schools to media to documentation to community leadership.

prompt: Some people think that all museums and art galleries should be free for visitors, paid for by public money. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Museums and art galleries hold some of a nation's most valuable cultural treasures, and the question of who should pay for them is often debated. I largely agree that entry should be free and funded by taxation, although I accept that special exhibitions and foreign tourists could reasonably be charged.

The strongest argument for free entry is equal access. A family on a low income may hesitate to spend a significant sum simply to look at paintings or fossils, so entrance fees quietly turn culture into a privilege of the well-off. When admission costs nothing, schoolchildren, pensioners and people who would never have planned a visit can walk in on impulse and discover an interest that lasts a lifetime. Since these collections were often acquired with public money or donated to the nation, it seems fair that the public should be able to see them without paying again.

Free museums also bring wider benefits. They support education by giving teachers a resource they can use repeatedly at no cost to parents, and they attract visitors who then spend money in nearby cafés, shops and hotels, which partly offsets the public expense. In addition, a lively cultural sector strengthens a city's reputation and encourages creative industries to locate there.

Nevertheless, public budgets are limited, and money spent on museums is not available for hospitals or schools. For this reason, a mixed model is sensible. Permanent collections should be free, whereas temporary exhibitions that are expensive to stage could charge a fee, and international tourists might pay a modest contribution.

In conclusion, I believe permanent museum collections should be free to visit and supported by public funds, as this opens culture to everyone and benefits the wider economy. Limited charges for special events, however, are a reasonable way to share the cost.

prompt: Advertising aimed at children under the age of twelve should be completely banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Children today are exposed to a constant stream of advertisements on television, video platforms and mobile games. I strongly agree that advertising directed at young children should be banned, because they cannot judge commercial messages fairly and the harms of such marketing outweigh its benefits.

The main reason is that young children do not fully understand what advertising is. Research in child development generally shows that younger children struggle to distinguish an advertisement from ordinary entertainment, and even when they can, they rarely recognise that its purpose is to persuade them. An adult knows that a cereal advert exaggerates; a six-year-old may simply believe that the product will make him stronger or more popular. Targeting people who cannot defend themselves against persuasion is, in my view, fundamentally unfair.

Furthermore, much of this advertising promotes products that are bad for children. Sugary snacks, fast food and drinks are heavily marketed with cartoon characters and free toys, contributing to unhealthy eating habits. Advertising also fuels so-called pester power: children repeatedly demand the latest toy or game, which creates conflict in families and puts pressure on parents with limited budgets.

Opponents argue that a ban would cut the income that funds children's television and that parents, not governments, should control what their children watch. However, quality children's programming can be financed through public broadcasting or subscriptions, and parents cannot realistically supervise every screen at every moment, particularly when adverts are embedded in games and online videos.

In conclusion, although a ban would have some financial costs for broadcasters, I believe it is justified. Young children deserve protection from persuasion they cannot understand, and removing such marketing would support healthier habits and calmer family life.

prompt: Some people believe that unpaid community service, such as helping in hospitals or cleaning parks, should be a compulsory part of secondary school education. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

In some countries, secondary pupils must complete a number of hours of volunteering before they graduate. I agree with this idea to a large extent, because community work teaches responsibility and practical skills that classrooms cannot provide, although the scheme should offer genuine choice and must not overload students.

The first benefit is the development of character. When teenagers read to elderly patients, coach younger children or help clear litter from a river bank, they see the direct effect of their effort on other people. This experience builds empathy and a sense of civic duty, and it can challenge the self-centred attitudes that adolescents are sometimes accused of. Pupils from comfortable backgrounds, in particular, may meet people whose lives are very different from their own.

Community service also brings practical advantages. Students learn to arrive on time, follow instructions and work with adults outside their family, which prepares them for the workplace. Many discover interests that shape their future; a pupil who helps in a hospital may decide to train as a nurse. In addition, charities and public services gain extra help, and the local area benefits from cleaner parks and better-supported residents.

Critics argue that compulsory volunteering is a contradiction and that students already face heavy academic pressure. These concerns are valid, but they can be addressed. If pupils choose from a wide range of activities and the required hours are modest, the work feels less like a punishment, and it need not take time away from essential study.

In conclusion, I believe a moderate requirement for community service in secondary schools is worthwhile. Provided that students have a choice of placements and the workload is reasonable, such a scheme benefits both young people and the communities they serve.

prompt: Some people believe that competitive sports at school teach children valuable lessons for life, while others think that competition does more harm than good to children who are not naturally athletic. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Most schools organise team games, races and tournaments, but there is disagreement about whether this competitive element helps or hurts pupils. In this essay I will consider both views, and I will argue that competition is valuable, provided it is balanced with activities in which every child can succeed.

Supporters of school competition point to the lessons it teaches. Children who play in a league learn to train regularly, cooperate with teammates and accept both victory and defeat with dignity. These experiences prepare them for adult life, where they will face job interviews, deadlines and setbacks. Moreover, competition motivates many pupils to try harder than they otherwise would, and the excitement of a match can make physical activity enjoyable rather than a chore.

On the other hand, critics argue that constant competition discourages children who are less talented. A pupil who is always picked last for a team or finishes at the back of every race may conclude that sport is not for them, and this can lead to a lifelong avoidance of exercise. In addition, public failure in front of classmates can damage self-esteem and even lead to teasing. As a result, the activity that was meant to promote health ends up having the opposite effect.

In my view, the answer is not to remove competition but to broaden it. Schools should offer non-competitive options such as dance, hiking and swimming for fitness, and they can group children by ability so that contests are more even. Furthermore, rewarding effort and improvement, not only winning, ensures that weaker players feel their progress is noticed.

In conclusion, competitive sport can build discipline and resilience, yet it may alienate pupils who lack natural ability. I believe schools should keep it, but within a wider programme that allows every child to enjoy being active.

prompt: Some people say that spending money on space exploration is a waste when there are so many problems on Earth, while others believe that it brings important benefits. model:
Every rocket launch costs vast sums, and critics ask why this money is not used to fight poverty or disease instead. Others insist that space research repays its cost many times over. Having considered both positions, I believe that space exploration is a worthwhile investment, although its budget should be kept in proportion to urgent needs at home.

Those who regard space programmes as wasteful make a powerful moral argument. Millions of people lack clean water, adequate healthcare or basic education, and a government that funds trips to Mars while its hospitals are underfunded appears to have the wrong priorities. In addition, the benefits of space missions can seem remote to ordinary citizens, as discovering ice on a distant moon does little to pay their rent.

However, this view underestimates how much everyday life depends on space technology. Satellites provide the weather forecasts that warn farmers and coastal towns of storms, the navigation systems in every smartphone, and much of the data scientists use to monitor deforestation, melting ice and crop failures. Research for space missions has also produced spin-off inventions in medical imaging, water purification and lightweight materials. Moreover, ambitious projects inspire young people to study science and engineering, building the skills a modern economy needs.

In my opinion, the choice is not as stark as critics suggest. Space budgets are a small part of public spending in most countries, so cancelling them would not solve global poverty. Nevertheless, governments should focus on missions with clear practical returns, such as Earth observation, and share the costs through international cooperation.

In conclusion, although the needs on our own planet are pressing, I believe space exploration should continue, since it delivers practical benefits and scientific progress that help solve some of those very problems.

prompt: Some people think that children are better off growing up in the countryside, while others believe that a city upbringing offers more advantages. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Parents who can choose where to raise their children often wonder whether a rural or an urban environment is better for them. Both settings offer distinct benefits, but in my view a city upbringing gives children more opportunities, provided they also have regular contact with nature.

Supporters of a rural childhood emphasise freedom and health. Children in the countryside can play outside with little traffic, explore fields and woods, and learn where food comes from by watching crops grow and animals being raised. Cleaner air and more physical activity help them stay fit, and smaller communities, in which neighbours know one another, can make young people feel safe and supported. Many adults remember such childhoods as calm and unhurried.

City advocates, by contrast, point to the range of opportunities available. Urban children usually have access to a wider choice of schools, libraries, museums, sports clubs and music lessons, which allows them to discover and develop particular talents. They also grow up among people of different backgrounds, languages and beliefs, which prepares them for a diverse adult world. In addition, better public transport lets older children travel independently, and specialist healthcare is closer at hand when it is needed.

On balance, I find the city's advantages more decisive, because educational and cultural opportunities shape a child's future in ways that are hard to replace. Rural families often have to drive long distances for activities that city children can reach by bus. The main weakness of urban life, the lack of green space, can be partly remedied by parks, weekend trips and holidays in the countryside.

In conclusion, a rural upbringing offers freedom and fresh air, whereas a city upbringing offers education and diversity. I believe the city is the better choice overall, as long as parents make sure their children still spend time in nature.

notes: Band 7: each view is developed with specific benefits rather than single adjectives, and the opinion paragraph explains why one set of advantages is more decisive and how the city's weakness can be reduced.

criteria.tr: Band 7 discusses both views fully and explains why the city's advantages are more decisive; band 6 states a preference ("more chances for their future") without developing it.

prompt: Some people believe that governments should tax sugary drinks and unhealthy foods to improve public health, while others argue that people should be free to decide what they eat. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Rising rates of obesity and diabetes have led several governments to introduce taxes on sugary drinks and similar products. Critics see these taxes as an intrusion into private life. Having weighed both views, I believe such taxes are justified, as long as they are combined with education and support for healthier choices.

Opponents of food taxes argue from the principle of personal freedom. Adults, they say, have the right to decide what they eat and drink, and the state should not punish them for choosing a fizzy drink or a chocolate bar. They also point out that these taxes fall most heavily on poorer households, which spend a larger share of their income on food. In their view, information campaigns would respect individual choice more than financial penalties.

Supporters, on the other hand, emphasise the wider costs of unhealthy diets. Diseases linked to excess sugar place a heavy burden on public health systems, which are funded by all taxpayers, so personal choices are not entirely private. A tax raises the price of the least healthy products and encourages manufacturers to reduce the sugar in their recipes to avoid it, which benefits even consumers who never think about nutrition. In addition, the revenue can pay for sports facilities, school meals or free drinking water.

In my opinion, the second argument is stronger, particularly where children are concerned, since they are heavily targeted by marketing and cannot judge long-term health risks. The concern about poorer families is valid, but it can be addressed by using the revenue to make fresh fruit and vegetables cheaper.

In conclusion, although freedom of choice matters, I believe governments should tax sugary and unhealthy products. When the money raised is spent on promoting healthy eating, such taxes protect public health without leaving people unable to choose.

notes: Band 7: the freedom argument is presented at its strongest (including the effect on poorer families) before being answered; the opinion is justified by the public cost of illness and the reformulation effect, and the main objection is resolved.

criteria.tr: Band 7 explains both views and answers the strongest objection; band 6 agrees with the tax but ignores the freedom argument it has just mentioned.

prompt: An increasing number of students choose to study at universities in other countries. Do the advantages of studying abroad outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Each year, more young people leave their home countries to earn a degree overseas. Studying abroad offers academic and personal benefits, but it also involves considerable cost and difficulty. In my view, for most students who can manage the expense, the advantages clearly outweigh the drawbacks.

The academic advantages are substantial. Students can attend universities with strong reputations in their chosen field, use modern laboratories and libraries, and learn from leading researchers. In addition, studying in another language, often English, brings a level of fluency that is hard to achieve at home. Employers value international graduates, as they tend to be adaptable and comfortable working with people from different cultures.

Personal growth is an equally important benefit. Living far from family forces young people to manage money, cook, deal with officials and solve problems on their own. They make friends from many countries and learn to see their own culture from the outside, which broadens their outlook in a way that no textbook can.

There are, however, real disadvantages. Tuition fees and living costs abroad can be extremely high, and families may take on heavy debts. Moreover, many students experience loneliness and culture shock, especially in the first months, and studying complex subjects in a second language can be exhausting. Their home country may also lose talented young people if they decide to stay overseas after graduating. Nevertheless, most of these problems are temporary or can be reduced. Scholarships and part-time work can ease the financial burden, and university support services help newcomers adjust. Many graduates who remain abroad still contribute to their home countries through business links and knowledge.

In conclusion, studying abroad is expensive and emotionally challenging, yet I believe its academic, professional and personal benefits outweigh these costs for students who prepare carefully.

prompt: Online shopping is replacing shopping in high-street stores in many countries. Do the advantages of this development outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
In many countries, a growing share of purchases is now made online rather than in traditional town-centre shops. This shift has made shopping more convenient and often cheaper, but it has also hurt local communities. Overall, I would argue that the advantages for consumers outweigh the disadvantages, although governments should act to protect town centres.

The most obvious advantage is convenience. Customers can browse thousands of products at any time of day, compare prices in seconds and have goods delivered to their door. This is especially valuable for people with disabilities, parents of young children and those living in rural areas far from large shops. Online competition also tends to lower prices, and customer reviews help buyers avoid poor-quality goods. For small producers, the internet offers access to customers around the world without the expense of renting a shop.

However, the decline of physical stores has serious consequences. As shops close, high streets lose their atmosphere and become lined with empty units, which discourages visitors and harms nearby cafés and services. Many retail jobs, often held by young or part-time workers, have disappeared. In addition, the growth in home deliveries increases van traffic and packaging waste, and frequent returns add further to the environmental cost. Some people, particularly the elderly, also miss the social contact that shopping in person provided.

Despite these drawbacks, the benefits reach almost every consumer, whereas many of the problems can be reduced. Town centres can be reinvented as places for leisure, culture and services that cannot be delivered, and stricter rules on packaging can limit waste.

In conclusion, the rise of online shopping has damaged traditional high streets and created environmental problems. On balance, however, I believe its advantages for consumers and small businesses are greater, provided town centres are adapted to new uses.
