prompt: In some countries, it is common for young people to take a year off between finishing school and starting university, often to travel or work. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Taking a gap year between school and university has become popular in a number of countries. Some young people use the time to travel, while others work or volunteer. I believe that, when the year is planned with a clear purpose, its advantages outweigh its disadvantages.

The main benefit is maturity. After years of following a school timetable, a period of independent work or travel teaches young people to organise their own time, handle money and cope with unfamiliar situations. As a result, many arrive at university more motivated and more certain about their choice of subject. A student who has spent several months working in a hospital, for instance, is likely to approach a medical degree with greater commitment than one who has never seen the profession in practice.

A gap year can also strengthen future employability. Paid work gives young people experience and references, and volunteering abroad develops language skills and cultural awareness that employers value. In addition, earning money before university can reduce the debts many students accumulate.

On the other hand, there are genuine risks. Without a plan, a year off can become a year of drifting, and some students lose the habit of study or decide not to return to education at all. International travel can be costly, so gap years may be available mainly to wealthier families, widening inequality. Furthermore, graduating a year later means starting a career, and earning a full salary, later than one's peers. Although these risks are real, they can be managed. A structured programme of work or volunteering, and a confirmed university place before the year begins, keep students on track.

In conclusion, a gap year carries some financial and academic risks. Nevertheless, I believe its benefits for maturity, motivation and employability outweigh them, provided that the year is used purposefully.

notes: Band 7: each advantage is explained through a consequence and an example, the disadvantages include a less obvious point (inequality), and the condition in the position ("planned with a clear purpose") is tied to how the risks are managed.

criteria.cc: Band 7 organises benefits into maturity and employability, then risks, then management; band 6 uses the formula "The advantage is... The disadvantage is...".

prompt: In many countries, cash is being replaced by card and mobile payments. Do the advantages of a cashless society outweigh the disadvantages? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Notes and coins are disappearing from daily life in many countries as people pay with cards and phones instead. A cashless economy is faster and safer in several ways, but it also excludes some groups and creates new risks. In my opinion, the advantages outweigh the disadvantages, provided that cash remains available for those who need it.

For consumers and businesses, digital payments are highly convenient. A purchase takes a second, there is no need to find an ATM or carry change, and every transaction is recorded automatically, which makes budgeting easier. Shops save the time and cost of counting, storing and transporting money, and they face a lower risk of robbery. Governments benefit as well: because electronic payments leave a record, it becomes harder to hide income from the tax authorities or to launder the proceeds of crime.

However, a world without cash has serious drawbacks. Elderly people, those with disabilities and people without bank accounts may struggle to pay for basic goods, and they risk being left behind. Electronic systems also depend on networks and electricity, so a technical failure or cyber-attack can make it impossible to buy food or fuel. In addition, every digital payment generates data about where and how people spend, which raises concerns about privacy and the power of banks and technology companies.

These problems are significant, but they can be addressed without abandoning digital payments. Governments can require shops to keep accepting cash for essential goods, offer free basic bank accounts and enforce strict rules on data protection and system security.

In conclusion, a cashless society brings speed, safety and greater transparency, while threatening to exclude vulnerable people and weaken privacy. On balance, I believe its benefits are greater, as long as cash continues to exist as a backup and personal data is properly protected.

prompt: The number of overweight children is rising in many countries. What are the causes of this problem, and what can be done to solve it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

The most direct cause is a change in diet. Processed snacks, fast food and sugary drinks are cheap, widely available and heavily advertised to young people, so many children consume far more calories than they need. Busy parents, who often work long hours, may rely on ready meals rather than cooking fresh food. At the same time, children are less active than previous generations. Instead of playing outside, many spend their free time on screens, and concerns about traffic and safety mean that fewer walk or cycle to school. Some schools have also reduced physical education to make room for academic subjects.

Solutions must therefore tackle both eating habits and exercise. Schools should provide nutritious meals, remove vending machines that sell sweets and fizzy drinks, and guarantee daily physical activity. Cooking lessons can teach pupils how to prepare simple, healthy dishes they can make at home. Governments can restrict advertising of unhealthy food to children and use taxes on sugary products to fund sports facilities. Local authorities, for their part, can build safe cycle routes and playgrounds so that being active becomes part of everyday life.

Parents remain crucial, as children copy the habits they see at home. Eating meals together, limiting screen time and taking part in active weekend pastimes as a family can make a lasting difference.

In conclusion, unhealthy diets and inactive lifestyles are the main causes of rising childhood obesity. To solve the problem, I believe that families, schools and governments must all play a part in reversing it, so coordinated action is needed to make healthy food and regular exercise the normal choice.

prompt: In many cities, older people who live alone suffer from loneliness. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to reduce it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.

Loneliness among older people harms both mental and physical health, and in my view it should be treated as a serious social problem that requires action from local authorities, communities and families.

Families are smaller and more mobile than in the past, so adult children frequently live in other cities or countries and can visit only occasionally. When a partner dies, an older person may suddenly find themselves alone in a home that once housed a busy family. Poor health and limited mobility make it difficult to go out, and the closure of local shops, post offices and community centres has removed many of the places where casual contact used to happen. Furthermore, the shift of services online can leave older people who are less confident with technology feeling cut off.

There are practical ways to reduce this isolation. First, local councils should fund community centres that offer affordable meals, classes and social activities, together with transport for those who cannot travel independently. Second, volunteer schemes can match older residents with people who visit or telephone them regularly, and intergenerational projects, such as students sharing housing with elderly homeowners, benefit both groups. Third, teaching older people to use video calls and messaging apps allows them to keep in touch with distant relatives. Finally, housing should be designed with shared gardens and common rooms, which encourage neighbours to meet naturally.

In conclusion, loneliness among the elderly in cities arises from family dispersal, bereavement, ill health and the loss of local meeting places. I believe it can be significantly reduced if councils, volunteers, families and planners work together to create opportunities for regular human contact.

prompt: Large amounts of plastic waste end up in the world's oceans. What are the main causes of this problem, and what can be done to tackle it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Plastic waste now floats on the surface of every ocean and washes up on even the most remote beaches, where it harms wildlife and may enter the food chain. The problem results from how plastic is produced, used and discarded, and I believe it can only be solved by reducing plastic use as well as improving waste management.

The root cause is the enormous quantity of single-use plastic. Bottles, bags, food containers and packaging are cheap and convenient, so they are used once and thrown away within minutes. Much of this waste is never recycled. In many developing countries, rapid growth in consumption has outpaced the construction of collection and disposal systems, so rubbish is dumped in open sites or rivers, which carry it to the sea. Wealthier countries share responsibility, because they have often exported their plastic waste to nations that lack the means to process it. In addition, fishing nets lost or abandoned at sea and tiny particles released from synthetic clothing in washing machines add to the pollution.

Tackling the issue requires action at several points. Governments should ban or tax unnecessary single-use items, such as plastic straws and carrier bags, and require manufacturers to take responsibility for the packaging they produce. Deposit schemes for bottles give consumers a financial reason to return them. International aid can help poorer countries build proper waste collection and recycling systems, and exports of plastic waste to countries that cannot manage it should be restricted. Finally, research into biodegradable materials and filters for washing machines can reduce pollution at its source.

In conclusion, ocean plastic is caused by excessive single-use packaging, inadequate waste systems and lost fishing gear. I believe the most effective response combines lower consumption, better waste management worldwide and responsibility for producers.

prompt: In many countries, a large number of young people are unable to find jobs after leaving school or university. What are the causes of youth unemployment, and what solutions can you suggest? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Many young people leave education full of hope, only to spend months or even years searching for work. High youth unemployment wastes talent and can lead to frustration and social unrest, so I believe it must be addressed through closer links between education and employers, as well as targeted government support.

One major cause is a mismatch between what young people learn and what employers need. Schools and universities often focus on academic knowledge, while companies are looking for practical, technical and communication skills. As a result, there may be a shortage of electricians or software testers at the same time as many graduates in other subjects cannot find suitable posts. A second cause is lack of experience. Employers prefer candidates who can be productive immediately, so school-leavers are trapped in a cycle in which they cannot get a job without experience and cannot gain experience without a job. Finally, economic downturns hit young workers hardest, as companies freeze recruitment before they dismiss existing staff.

Several measures could improve the situation. First, governments and businesses should expand apprenticeships and vocational courses, which combine study with paid work and lead directly to qualifications employers recognise. Second, universities should offer internships and careers advice from the first year, helping students choose courses with good prospects. Third, tax incentives can encourage firms to hire and train young employees, especially during recessions. In addition, support for young entrepreneurs, such as small loans and mentoring, can help some create their own jobs.

In conclusion, youth unemployment stems mainly from a skills mismatch, the experience trap and economic cycles. I believe that stronger cooperation between education and industry, supported by government incentives, offers the most effective way to help young people into work.

prompt: Some people believe that working from home is the best option for employees. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

While some people argue that it harms young people's mental health, others point to its social and educational benefits. On balance, I believe that the benefits can outweigh the risks, provided that young people use these platforms carefully and with guidance.

Those who criticise social media often point to its effect on self-esteem. Teenagers constantly compare their appearance and achievements with carefully edited images online, which can lead to anxiety and low confidence. Furthermore, excessive use may disrupt sleep and reduce the time spent on exercise or face-to-face friendships.

Nevertheless, social media can also provide significant advantages. It allows young people to keep in touch with friends who live far away, to find communities that share their interests, and to access educational material that was once difficult to obtain. For teenagers who feel isolated at school, online groups can offer valuable support and a sense of belonging. Schools that use online platforms for homework and debate, for example, can help students build research skills that they will need at university. Young people who share their work online also gain practical experience of writing for an audience, which many employers value. Such benefits are most valuable when the platforms are used with adult guidance rather than left unsupervised.

In conclusion, although social media can damage young people's wellbeing, I believe that its benefits are substantial. Parents and schools should therefore teach teenagers how to use these platforms responsibly rather than banning them outright.
notes: Band 7: both views are presented fairly before the writer's own position; the harm paragraph and the benefit paragraph each carry a specific example. Band 6 essays describe both views but give the opinion only in the last sentence, with no link to the body.
band6: Some people think social media is bad for teenagers because they get sad. Others think it is good because they can talk to friends. I think both are true. Teenagers should use it carefully. In conclusion, social media has good and bad sides.

criteria.tr: Band 7 presents both views with development and states an opinion with a condition; band 6 names both views and gives an opinion without developing either.
criteria.cc: Band 7 uses a clear order (views, harm, benefit, opinion) with cohesive devices such as 'Furthermore' and 'Nevertheless'; band 6 uses 'Some people' and 'Others' without developing a sequence.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'sharply divided', 'carefully edited images' and 'a sense of belonging'; band 6 uses 'bad' and 'good' repeatedly.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses relative clauses, concessive structures and passive forms accurately; band 6 uses short sentences with little variety.

prompt: Some people believe that the advantages of tourism outweigh its disadvantages for local communities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
model:
Tourism is often promoted as a route to prosperity for towns and regions that lack other industries. In my view, the economic and cultural gains from visitors are real and substantial, but they are not always greater than the costs, particularly where tourism is poorly planned. I believe the balance depends on how the industry is managed.

The main advantage is economic. Visitors spend money on hotels, restaurants and transport, which creates jobs for local people who might otherwise have to move to cities to find work. Tourist income can also fund the upkeep of historic buildings, museums and parks that residents enjoy themselves. In addition, shops and services in quieter areas often survive thanks to the extra custom that visitors bring.

However, the disadvantages can be serious. Popular destinations may suffer from traffic congestion, rising rents and a shortage of housing as homes are converted into holiday rentals. Local traditions can also be reshaped to suit visitors rather than residents, and seasonal jobs are often low-paid and insecure. When these problems grow, residents may feel that their own town belongs to tourists. Residents who depend on seasonal work also face uncertainty when visitor numbers fall during bad weather or economic downturns. Such fluctuations make it harder for families to plan their finances over the long term.

In conclusion, tourism brings clear economic and cultural benefits to local communities, but these benefits outweigh the costs only when visitor numbers are controlled and residents share in the profits. Governments should therefore limit the growth of mass tourism and invest the income in housing and services.
notes: Band 7: the answer states a conditional position, develops the advantage with three linked points, then sets out the disadvantages and returns to the condition in the conclusion. Band 6 essays list benefits and harms without weighing them against each other.
band6: Tourism is good because people spend money and jobs are created. But tourism is also bad because there are too many people and prices go up. Local people do not like it. In conclusion, tourism has advantages and disadvantages for the community.

criteria.tr: Band 7 gives a conditional position, develops the main advantage and weighs it against the disadvantages; band 6 lists both sides without weighing them.
criteria.cc: Band 7 uses paragraphs for advantage, disadvantage and conclusion with signposts such as 'In addition' and 'However'; band 6 uses 'but' and 'because' between short sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'a route to prosperity', 'reshaped to suit visitors' and 'insecure'; band 6 uses 'good', 'bad' and 'too many people'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses conditional and concessive clauses and passive forms ('are converted into', 'be reshaped'); band 6 relies on simple sentences.

prompt: In many cities, traffic noise and construction work create serious problems for residents. What are the causes of this problem and what solutions can you suggest?
model:
Noise pollution has become a serious concern in many cities, and residents often find it hard to sleep or concentrate at home. The main causes are heavy traffic and building work, and I believe that authorities can reduce the problem through better planning and stricter controls.

Road traffic is the most persistent source of noise. Cars, buses and lorries pass through residential streets at all hours, and motorcycles and sirens add to the din. Construction work forms a second major source, as drilling and demolition continue for long periods, often into the evening. Both sources are worse in dense districts, where buildings reflect sound and leave few quiet corners.

Authorities can tackle traffic noise by restricting heavy vehicles to ring roads at night and by installing low-noise road surfaces on busy streets. Construction firms should be required to work within set hours and to use quieter equipment. Planners can also protect homes by placing parks, offices and shops along the busiest routes, which act as a buffer between traffic and houses. Night-time noise is especially damaging, since people who are kept awake regularly find it harder to work the following day. Children in noisy homes may also struggle to study, which can affect their results at school. Local councils that collect complaints can use the data to identify the streets where action is most urgently needed.

In conclusion, traffic and construction are the main sources of urban noise. I believe that these can be controlled through tighter rules on working hours, quieter technology and smarter planning, which would protect residents' health and sleep.
notes: Band 7: causes are separated from solutions; each cause is explained in terms of where and when it happens, and each solution is matched to a cause and an actor. Band 6 essays list causes and solutions in one paragraph without matching them.
band6: There is too much noise in cities. The cars make noise and the buildings make noise. To solve this, the government should make rules. Builders should work at certain times. People can also plant trees. In conclusion, noise is a big problem.

criteria.tr: Band 7 separates causes from solutions, explains when and where each cause operates and matches each solution to an actor; band 6 mentions causes and solutions in general terms.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each cause and each solution its own paragraph, with topic sentences; band 6 mixes causes and solutions in the same sentences.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'persistent source', 'dense districts' and 'a buffer between traffic and houses'; band 6 uses 'a big problem' and 'make noise'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses participle clauses ('leave few quiet corners') and passive modals ('should be required'); band 6 repeats 'there is' and simple modal structures.

prompt: Some people think that public libraries should be funded by the government, while others argue they should be run by private companies. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
model:
Public libraries have long been a cornerstone of community life, and there is disagreement about who should own and manage them. Some argue that public funding is the only way to keep libraries open for everyone, while others believe that private firms could run them more efficiently. In my opinion, libraries should remain publicly funded, but managers could learn from private operators in how they serve users.

Those who favour government funding point out that libraries provide free access to books, computers and learning resources, regardless of income. Their services, such as literacy classes for adults and reading groups for children, rarely make a profit and would therefore disappear under commercial control. Public ownership also keeps decisions accountable to residents rather than to shareholders.

Advocates of private management, however, argue that companies can bring modern business methods, longer opening hours and new sources of income, such as cafés and events. Competition for contracts could drive down costs and free money for new books and digital services. Such arrangements have worked in some places, although they require careful monitoring to protect the core services. Commercial operators may also reduce opening hours in quiet periods, leaving communities with fewer services when they need them most. A public library, by contrast, is expected to remain open for everyone at fixed times, regardless of how busy it is.

In conclusion, while private firms may offer useful ideas, I believe that public libraries serve a social purpose that the market cannot guarantee. Governments should keep ownership and funding, and they should adopt the efficient practices that private managers have shown can work.
notes: Band 7: each view receives its own paragraph with reasons and an example, and the writer's opinion keeps public ownership while borrowing the useful part of the other view. Band 6 essays describe the two views and then repeat their own opinion without a link.
band6: Libraries should be paid for by the government because they are free for everyone. But private companies can also run libraries and make them better. I think the government should pay but companies can help. In conclusion, both ideas are good.

criteria.tr: Band 7 develops both views with reasons and an example and gives a reasoned opinion that borrows from each side; band 6 names the views and gives a general opinion.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives each view its own paragraph and links them with 'however' and 'while'; band 6 joins both views with 'but' in one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'accountable to residents', 'drive down costs' and 'regardless of income'; band 6 uses 'good', 'better' and 'paid for'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses concessive, result and purpose clauses and passive modals ('should be kept'); band 6 writes mostly simple sentences.

prompt: Many cities are spending heavily on public transport, yet road building continues and many commuters still drive to work. Is this the right balance? What measures could make public transport more attractive to commuters? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Urban authorities have poured money into buses and trains in recent years, but motorways keep expanding and car travel remains the norm. In my view, the balance is not yet right, because new roads mainly encourage more car use. I believe that governments should shift investment towards buses, trams and cycle lanes, and make public transport the easiest choice for daily travel.

New roads often fill with traffic within a few years, a pattern that planners call induced demand. When journeys become faster by car, more people choose to drive, and congestion returns. Public transport, by contrast, can move large numbers of passengers along a single corridor, which makes it far more space-efficient in dense areas.

Several measures could make public transport more attractive. Frequent services with reliable timetables would reduce waiting times, while integrated tickets would allow passengers to switch between buses and trains with one payment. Safe and direct routes for cyclists could also link homes to stations, so that residents can combine modes easily. Bus rapid transit lines in many cities have shown how quickly ridership can rise once service becomes frequent. Park-and-ride sites at the edge of town would also let drivers switch to buses before the most congested streets, which removes cars from the centre. Such schemes show that good connections matter as much as frequency. Fare caps, which limit the total spent in a week, can also make regular travel by public transport cheaper than driving.

In conclusion, road building can relieve congestion only briefly, whereas investment in public transport offers lasting benefits. Governments should therefore prioritise reliable, affordable services and connect them with safe cycling routes.
notes: Band 7: the answer gives a position on the balance, explains induced demand as the reason roads fail, and lists measures that each address a specific problem. Band 6 answers name measures in one list without explaining how each one changes behaviour.
band6: Public transport is good and roads are bad because of traffic. Governments should build more buses and trains. They should make tickets cheaper and have more trains. People will use them more. In conclusion, public transport is better than cars.

criteria.tr: Band 7 answers both questions directly, explains the mechanism behind the position and proposes measures tied to specific problems; band 6 lists measures without explaining them.
criteria.cc: Band 7 separates the balance question from the measures question in separate paragraphs and links them in the conclusion; band 6 blends the questions into one paragraph.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'induced demand', 'space-efficient' and 'integrated tickets'; band 6 uses 'good', 'bad' and 'cheaper'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses result and contrast clauses ('whereas investment ... offers') and modal verbs of recommendation; band 6 uses simple sentences with 'should' only.

prompt: Plastic packaging is widely used in supermarkets, but it creates large amounts of waste. Is plastic packaging a serious problem for the environment? What should governments and businesses do to reduce it? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Plastic packaging keeps food fresh and reduces spoilage, yet it also fills landfills and oceans with waste that lasts for generations. In my view, plastic packaging is a serious environmental problem, and I believe that both governments and businesses must act to reduce its use rather than simply encouraging recycling.

Packaging is a major source of household waste, and much of it is used for only a few minutes before being thrown away. Recycling rates remain low in many places, partly because mixed plastics are difficult to sort and clean, so large quantities end up in incinerators or are abandoned in the environment. Small fragments can also enter rivers and seas, where they harm wildlife.

Governments can reduce plastic use through deposit schemes that return money for bottles, bans on single-use items and taxes on packaging that is hard to recycle. Businesses can redesign products with less material, offer refill stations in shops, and use paper or plant-based alternatives where they perform as well. A supermarket that sells loose produce, for example, can cut packaging considerably without losing customers. Consumers also respond to clear labels that explain how a product can be recycled or refilled, and they are more likely to buy packaging that is easy to reuse. Retailers that introduce refill schemes often find that customers return regularly once the habit is established. Such measures also create demand for new materials, which encourages investment in reuse systems.

In conclusion, plastic packaging creates lasting harm that recycling alone cannot solve. Governments should introduce firm rules and incentives, while businesses should redesign packaging so that less plastic is produced in the first place.
notes: Band 7: the position separates recycling from reduction, the body gives the mechanism of harm, and the solutions are split by actor with one concrete example. Band 6 answers say plastic is bad and recommend recycling without distinguishing the actors.
band6: Plastic is bad for the environment because it is in the sea. Governments should make laws and shops should sell less plastic. People should recycle more. In conclusion, plastic is a problem and we must stop using it.

criteria.tr: Band 7 gives a position that distinguishes reduction from recycling, explains the harm and proposes solutions for each actor; band 6 gives generic solutions.
criteria.cc: Band 7 gives the harm, then governments, then businesses, with an example in the middle of the business paragraph; band 6 mixes the actors in one list.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'incinerators', 'deposit schemes' and 'considerably without losing customers'; band 6 uses 'bad', 'stop' and 'a problem'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses passive forms ('are abandoned', 'is produced') and a range of modal verbs; band 6 uses simple present statements.

prompt: Many young people leave school without clear career plans. Is this a failure of the education system? What changes could help students prepare for work? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
A large number of school-leavers have no clear idea of the careers they want to pursue, and some drift through several jobs before settling down. This is partly a failure of the education system, but I believe that schools, families and employers all share responsibility for preparing students for work.

Schools focus heavily on exam results and academic subjects, which leaves little time for pupils to explore different occupations. Many students receive little guidance on how qualifications connect to jobs, and those from families without professional contacts have fewer opportunities to learn about work first-hand. As a result, choices made at sixteen or eighteen may rest on limited information.

Several changes could help. Schools could introduce regular work experience placements, invite professionals to talk about their jobs, and give careers advisers time to meet every student. Employers could offer apprenticeships and mentoring schemes, while parents could be encouraged to treat vocational training as an equally valuable route. A student who spends a week in a hospital or a workshop often gains more clarity than a year of classroom advice. Careers fairs that bring together local employers and former students can also show young people the range of options open to them. Such events are most useful when they start early, before students choose their subjects. Students who see the link between a subject and a job tend to take their studies more seriously.

In conclusion, the difficulty lies in gaps in support rather than in a lack of ambition among young people. Schools, employers and families should therefore work together to give students practical experience and clear information about career options.
notes: Band 7: the answer apportions responsibility without simply blaming schools, explains the mechanism (exam focus and unequal access to work contacts), and proposes changes for each actor. Band 6 answers blame schools and list generic advice.
band6: Schools do not teach students about jobs. They only teach exams. Students should find out about jobs. Parents can help too. Employers could give work experience. In conclusion, young people need more help with careers.

criteria.tr: Band 7 apportions responsibility across three actors, explains why students lack information and gives an example; band 6 blames one actor and gives generic advice.
criteria.cc: Band 7 moves from the problem to the cause to the solutions, with each actor in its own sentence group; band 6 repeats 'should' sentences in one block.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'drift through', 'first-hand' and 'vocational training'; band 6 uses 'help', 'find out' and 'more help'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses concessive and result clauses ('but I believe', 'As a result') and relative clauses; band 6 relies on simple sentences.

prompt: Fast food is cheap and convenient, but many people eat it regularly despite its health risks. Is this a personal choice or a problem for society? What measures could governments take to encourage healthier eating? Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience.
model:
Fast food is cheap, quick and widely available, yet regular consumption is linked to obesity and heart disease. This is partly a matter of personal choice, but I believe that governments have a responsibility to make healthier eating easier, since many people lack the time or money to cook from scratch.

Individuals certainly decide what they eat, yet the environment shapes those decisions. Fast food outlets cluster near schools and offices, and their advertising is often aimed at children. Large portions are frequently cheaper than healthier options, so low-income families may find that the least expensive food is also the least nutritious.

Governments could respond in several ways. Clear calorie labels on menus would help customers compare options, while limits on advertising to children could reduce the appeal of sugary products. Taxes on sugary drinks have been introduced in some countries, and the income can fund school meals and sports facilities. Employers could also support healthier choices by subsidising canteen meals. Schools could also teach practical cooking in place of some lessons, so that pupils learn how to prepare simple meals at home. Such lessons give children skills they will use throughout their lives, and they are inexpensive to run. A school that serves balanced lunches and removes vending machines can change the habits of an entire community. Such habits are easier to form in childhood than to change later in life.

In conclusion, eating fast food is a personal decision, but its health costs fall on society as a whole. Governments should therefore combine clear information, fair pricing and restrictions on marketing to make healthier eating the easy option.
notes: Band 7: the answer splits personal choice from environmental pressure, shows how pricing and placement shape the choice, and gives three measures with a stated effect. Band 6 answers call it a personal choice and list generic government actions.
band6: Fast food is bad for health. People should choose healthy food. The government can put prices on fast food and make adverts stop. Schools can teach children about food. In conclusion, fast food is a problem for everybody.

criteria.tr: Band 7 splits personal choice from environmental pressure and gives measures with stated effects; band 6 gives a generic opinion and generic measures.
criteria.cc: Band 7 moves from the position to the mechanism to the measures and conclusion, with contrast signposts ('certainly ... yet'); band 6 uses one sentence per idea with no signposts.
criteria.lr: Band 7 uses 'cluster near', 'subsidising' and 'the appeal of sugary products'; band 6 uses 'bad', 'choose' and 'a problem'.
criteria.gra: Band 7 uses concessive clauses ('Individuals certainly decide ... yet'), passive forms and modal verbs of recommendation; band 6 uses simple statements.
